Trumpet (Doctrine)
TRUM-pet
n.
From Old French trompette; Hebrew chatsōts’rāh (silver trumpet) and shōphār (ram’s horn); Greek salpinx. The trumpet is one of the most extensive musical-and-signaling instruments in Scripture, used for war, worship, civic gathering, and eschatological signal.

📖 Biblical Definition

The trumpet is one of the most extensive musical-and-signaling instruments in Scripture, used across both testaments for several distinct purposes. Several biblical uses anchor the doctrine. First, the silver trumpets of the priests. Numbers 10:1-10 prescribes two silver trumpets for the priests to use in calling the assembly, in directing the camps’ journeys, in announcing alarm before going to battle, and in the days of gladness, solemn days, and beginnings of months. The silver trumpets had specific signal-patterns for specific purposes: one trumpet for the princes, two for the whole assembly, alarm-blasts for journey, alarm-blasts for war. Second, the ram’s horn shophar. The shophar, simpler than the silver trumpet and more piercing in sound, was used for civic-religious signals throughout OT Israel. It announced the Year of Jubilee (Lev 25:9); it sounded at the giving of the Law at Sinai (and the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, Ex 19:19); it called Israel to assemble for war (Judg 3:27; 6:34; Neh 4:18-20); it announced the coronation of kings; it summoned the people to repentance (Joel 2:1, 15); it was the central instrument of the Feast of Trumpets (Lev 23:24). Third, the trumpet of victory at Jericho. Joshua 6 records the seven priests bearing seven trumpets of ram’s horns marching around Jericho once a day for six days, and seven times on the seventh day, with the great shout-and-trumpet-blast at which the walls fell down flat. The trumpet of Jericho is the OT’s great demonstration of the LORD’s use of the trumpet-blast as the means of His own deliverance, with no human military-power doing the work. Fourth, the eschatological trumpet. The supreme NT use is the trumpet of Christ’s return. 1 Corinthians 15:52: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. 1 Thessalonians 4:16: for the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first. Matthew 24:31: and he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds. Revelation 8-11 includes the seven trumpets of judgment, the trumpets through which the LORD’s judgments are announced and executed in the apocalyptic vision. The trumpet-doctrine therefore carries substantial theological substance across the canon: the priestly silver trumpets for orderly worship and signal; the ram’s horn for civic-religious and martial gathering; the trumpet of Jericho as the LORD’s own instrument of deliverance; the Year of Jubilee’s release-trumpet; and supremely the eschatological trumpet of the Lord’s return that gathers the elect, raises the dead in Christ, transforms the living, and inaugurates the consummation of all things.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TRUMPET as a wind instrument of music, in the form of a long tube curved at one or two places; in scripture, the most extensive musical-and-signaling instrument, used for war, worship, civic gathering (silver trumpets, ram’s horn shophar), the Year of Jubilee, and supremely the eschatological trumpet of the Lord’s return (1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16; Matt 24:31).

TRUMPET, n. — A wind instrument of music, in the form of a long tube curved at one or two places. In scripture, the most extensive musical-and-signaling instrument, with several types (silver trumpet, ram’s horn shophar) used for war, worship, civic gathering, the Year of Jubilee, and the eschatological signal of the Lord’s return.

SHOPHAR, n. — The ram’s horn trumpet of OT Israel, used for civic-religious-and-martial signals; the central instrument of the Feast of Trumpets (Lev 23:24) and the Year of Jubilee (Lev 25:9).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 15:52 — "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed."

1 Thessalonians 4:16 — "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first."

Numbers 10:1-2 — "And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, Make thee two trumpets of silver; of a whole piece shalt thou make them: that thou mayest use them for the calling of the assembly, and for the journeying of the camps."

Joshua 6:20 — "So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The trumpet-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the general loss of attention to OT musical-and-signaling-instrument detail that has muted the substantive theological substance the various trumpet-references carry—and on the other by speculative-date-setting traditions that have attempted to pinpoint the last-trump of Christ’s return to specific calendar dates, against the apostolic restraint and Christ’s explicit teaching that no man knoweth the day or hour.

expand to see more

The general loss of attention to OT musical-and-signaling-instrument detail has muted substantive theological substance the various trumpet-references carry. The silver trumpets of Numbers 10 had specific signal-patterns for specific purposes; the shophar of Jericho was the LORD’s instrument of deliverance; the Year of Jubilee’s trumpet announced release; the Feast of Trumpets inaugurated the most sacred month; each carries pastoral and theological weight that the contemporary preaching often skips. The recovery is the recovery of attention to the biblical instruments and their signal-functions: the trumpet’s call to assemble (Num 10), to repent (Joel 2), to release captives (Lev 25:9, the Jubilee trumpet typologically anticipating Christ’s announcement of the acceptable year of the Lord), to fight under the LORD’s deliverance (Jericho), to worship in the appointed Feast of Trumpets—all carrying their own theological substance the contemporary inattention has obscured.

The opposite contemporary corruption is the speculative-date-setting tradition that has attempted to pinpoint the last-trump of Christ’s return to specific calendar dates (often tied to the Jewish Feast of Trumpets in particular years). Christ’s explicit teaching forecloses this: but of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only (Matt 24:36). The typological connection between the OT Feast of Trumpets and the eschatological last-trump is real; the inference to a specific calendar date is forbidden. The recovery is the recovery of both ends: the substantive typological-eschatological doctrine (the last-trump is real, the LORD’s return is certain, the dead in Christ will be raised at the trumpet’s sound, the elect will be gathered) and the apostolic restraint (the date is not given to us, and speculative attempts to calculate it are not the right response). The Christian waits, watches, and prepares for the trumpet’s sound in faithful daily discipleship, hearing in the OT trumpets the typological echo of the great eschatological trumpet to come, and waiting in patient expectation for the Lord who will descend from heaven with the trump of God when the Father’s appointed hour has come.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chatsōts’rāh (silver trumpet) and shōphār (ram’s horn); Greek salpinx (trumpet); the most extensive musical-and-signaling instrument in Scripture, used for war (Jericho), worship (Feast of Trumpets, daily-continual-offerings), civic gathering (assembly-calls), the Year of Jubilee’s release-announcement, and supremely the eschatological trumpet of Christ’s return that raises the dead in Christ and gathers the elect.

Hebrew chatsōts’rāh (H2689) — silver trumpet (Num 10:1-10).

Hebrew shōphār (H7782) — ram’s horn trumpet (over 70 OT uses).

Greek salpinx (G4536) — trumpet (11 NT uses; 1 Cor 14:8; 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16; Heb 12:19; Rev 1:10; 4:1; 8:2, 6, 13; 9:14).

Greek salpizō (G4537) — to sound a trumpet (12 NT uses; Matt 6:2; Rev 8-9-10-11 of the seven-trumpet judgments).
